name: btdu
desc: Sampling disk usage profiler for btrfs
why: A sampling disk usage profiler for btrfs that estimates space statistically, a clever idea that exposes filesystem internals.

brief.what_it_is: btdu is a terminal disk usage profiler for btrfs filesystems, written in D. Instead of walking every file, it picks random points on the disk in use, finds what owns each point, and adds that path to a tree. It takes a mounted btrfs filesystem path (which must be the top-level subvolume) and shows a browsable, interactive tree of estimated sizes. It can also run headless and print a tree to stdout, or export results to .btdu (binary) or .json files, and compare a live run against a saved baseline. Sizes are statistical estimates that become more accurate the longer it runs.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says btrfs features like subvolumes, file and extent cloning, and compression make classic analyzers such as ncdu unable to give an accurate picture of actual disk usage. Sampling sidesteps that by asking the filesystem what is at random points, so results appear instantly and converge over time.
brief.how_it_works: Each sample picks a random point on the used disk, resolves what is located there, and records the path; the README says it queries raw filesystem metadata, which is why it needs root. An extent shared by several files or snapshots is placed at the shortest path (ties broken lexicographically), so each extent is counted once. The README describes eventual accuracy and says roughly 100 samples give about 1% resolution.

brief.install_notes: Besides brew, the README lists a package-manager install where packaged, static binaries on the GitHub releases page or the latest CI run, and a Nix flake. Source builds need a D compiler, Dub, and the ncurses wide-character development library (libncursesw5-dev on Debian-family systems). The README warns that not all distributions package compatible versions of the dependencies, so success is not guaranteed for manual builds; it recommends Nix in that case. Running it requires root, and the target must be the top-level subvolume, or you must remount with -o subvol=/,subvolid=5. Recent versions also offer --auto-mount for non-top-level mounts. No accounts or runtimes are needed beyond that.
brief.standout: Its sampling approach gives usable answers almost immediately and handles snapshots, reflinks, and compression without special cases. The README also says it can estimate unreachable 'dark matter' extent space, which it calls a feature unique to btdu, and the shortest-path placement lets snapshot sizes be read as the amount of new data.
brief.status: Maintained. The GitHub releases page shows v0.7.2 marked Latest, dated 05 Jan (the year is not shown in the fetched text), preceded by v0.7.1 on 02 Jan and v0.7.0 on 01 Jan, with a steady history back to v0.3.1. The v0.7.0 notes say btdu is feature complete relative to its original vision and that it is the last major release before 1.0. I did not check commit history.
brief.caveats: Requires root privileges, because it reads raw btrfs metadata. It analyses whole filesystems only, with no way to restrict a run to one subdirectory or subvolume. Early results are wildly inaccurate and only settle with time. Deleting files outside btdu during a run skews the numbers until you restart sampling. Manual builds can fail on mismatched dependencies. Licensed GPL v2, inherited from btrfs-progs. The Homebrew package has no caveats of its own. The README's See Also section names btsdu, a similar btrfs snapshot analyzer.
quotes: btdu needs to collect only 100 samples to achieve a ~1% resolution, which means it can identify space hogs very quickly.
Though it works by taking random samples, it is "eventually" accurate.
A feature unique to btdu is the ability to estimate the amount of space used by unreachable parts of extents
